original: This chapter changes the question. Instead of asking how to build an agent out of a market, it asks what a market computes. The first section starts from probabilities rather than prices. It shows that the natural way to optimize a probability distribution, mirror ascent, is the same thing as continuous-time Bayesian updating, so that a reward signal acts on a learner exactly as a stream of evidence would, evidence that makes itself true. The following sections then define a production economy on a directed graph and derive the equations for its prices. These \emph{price recursion} equations turn out to be backpropagation when the economy is a chain of factories, the Bellman equation when it merely passes goods along, and Bayesian inference when routing shares are updated by mirror ascent. The conclusion is that an agent's reward is not an arbitrary input but the price that the surrounding economy sets on what it does. Price recursion is to reward what Bayes' rule is to evidence. The chapter ends with the \texttt{marketgrad} library, which implements these markets and checks the identities numerically. The two sections are adapted from informal articles and keep much of their first-person style.

original: This chapter brings that question back to the economics of \cref{part:agency}. There, a market was a machine for computing values: price recursion carried the value of final consumption back through the economy, so that every intermediate good was priced by what it eventually contributed. The arbitrage metric of \cref{ch:consistency} looks like a different kind of object, a static measure of incoherence. The first half of this chapter shows that it is not different at all. The arbitrage metric is exactly the welfare that a market of consumers gains by trading, its arbitraged forecasts are the market's equilibrium prices, and the price recursion of \cref{ch:agency} decomposes the global arbitrageur into many local ones. Along the way, preferences and beliefs turn out to be aggregated by the same rule: the ``utilitarian welfare'' assumed in \cref{ch:agency} is the arbitrage-free combination of utilities read as beliefs.

original: The second half turns this observation on latent variables. In a market over dependent questions, a latent variable is simply an \emph{intermediate good}. Nobody consumes it and it never resolves, but it is priced by everything downstream of it, and the market's adjustment rule turns out to be the EM algorithm. So price recursion does put a value on latent beliefs. What it does not settle is \emph{which} latent structure the market should hold, because many latent models predict the observables equally well. We therefore ask what gives a latent belief its meaning when only observables can be scored. The answer we develop is that a latent means exactly what it does to predictions of observables, that what is left over splits into a harmless part (a choice of coordinates) and a genuine part, and that the genuine part can be removed by asking latents to explain the observables cheaply. This gives a scoring rule, the \emph{tempered log score}, whose expected value is maximized by the most economical latent explanation. We close by using these results to assess the existing proposals for latent-variable prediction markets.
raw: The second half of the chapter studies latent variables in prediction markets. Latent variables in markets on dependent questions play the role of intermediate goods: they are never consumed (observed) but have prices determined by downstream questions, and the market dynamics amount to the EM algorithm. We see how price recursion gives meaning to beliefs about latent variables, but not [[\emph{which}}] beliefs: since many latent variable models predict observables equally well, the market has no way of choosing between them. We suggest that the meaning of a latent variable is what it predicts about observables, that the degrees of freedom not fixed by observables decompose into benign and substantive ones, and that substantive degrees of freedom can be fixed by demanding parsimony in latent-variable explanations of observed quantities. This leads us to a new scoring rule, the [[\emph{tempered log score}]], whose expectation is maximized by the most parsimonious explanation of observables. We close by commenting on previously proposed market designs for latent variables.
humanized: The second half of the paper is about latent variables. Latent variables are those that agents do not directly consume or care about, but are relevant for predicting variables that they do care about (i.e. latent variables matter only through their effect on other variables). In a market over dependent questions, a latent variable is simply an \emph{intermediate good}. We show that the price recursion still makes sense when there are latent variables (though of course prices can only be assigned to the non-latent variables), and the resulting price adjustment procedure is the EM algorithm. What it does not settle is \emph{which} latent structure the market should hold, because many latent models predict the observables equally well. We then discuss what it means for a belief over a latent variable to be correct, given that only the non-latent variables can be scored. We show that the meaning of a belief over latent variables is exactly captured by its predictions for the non-latent variables, and that any further notion of correctness can be divided into two parts: an arbitrary (but harmless) part that amounts to a choice of coordinates for the latent variables, and a substantive part, which can be eliminated by requiring that latent variables parsimoniously explain the non-latent variables. This gives a scoring rule, the \emph{tempered log score}, whose expected value is maximized by the most economical latent explanation. We then apply our characterization to existing proposals for prediction markets with latent variables.

So price recursion does put a value on beliefs about latent variables. What it does not settle is \emph{which} latent structure the market should hold, because many latent models predict the observables equally well. We therefore ask what gives a belief over a latent variable its meaning, given that only the observables can be scored. We argue that the meaning of a belief over latent variables is exactly captured by its predictions for the observables, and that what is left over can be divided into two parts: an arbitrary (but harmless) part that amounts to a choice of coordinates for the latent variables, and a substantive part, which can be eliminated by requiring that latent variables explain the observables parsimoniously. For a distribution [[$\mu$]] over [[$\Omega$]], let [[$M_i(\mu)$]] be the probability that question [[$x_i$]] is not voided and let [[$\mu_i$]] be the distribution of its answer given that it is not voided. Then

original: Read this way, the arbitrageur's worst-case distribution over worlds is itself a coherent belief, and the arbitrage metric is how far, in total KL divergence, the forecaster's beliefs are from the nearest coherent one. In information-geometric terms it is an I-projection (a ``reverse KL'' projection) of the forecasts onto the set of consistent beliefs. The proposition also explains the convention in \cref{ch:consistency} of scoring voided questions as zero: it weights a conditional question by the probability of its condition.

\begin{example}\label{arb:ex:election}
A forecaster gives both the Democratic and the Republican candidate a 60\% chance of winning, and exactly one of them will win. Write both forecasts as distributions over the two worlds: $p_1=(0.6,0.4)$ and $p_2=(0.4,0.6)$, with $b_1=b_2=1$. The geometric pool is $q^*=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$, and the arbitrage metric is
\[
A=\KL(q^*\|p_1)+\KL(q^*\|p_2)=-2\log\!\big(2\sqrt{0.24}\big)\approx0.041\ \text{nats},
\]
which agrees with the closed form for the negation check given in \cref{cfc:sec:arbitrage}.
\end{example}

The right-hand side of \eqref{arb:eq:jensen} is the gap in Jensen's inequality for the convex function $\Phi$, a quantity known as the \emph{Bregman information} \citep{banerjeeClusteringBregmanDivergences2005}. The Hessian of $\Phi$ is the covariance matrix of the softmax distribution, so for small disagreements
\[
A\approx\frac B2\sum_iw_i\Var_{q^*}\!\big(U_i-\Ubar\big),\qquad\text{and for a binary question}\quad A\approx\frac B2\,q^*(1-q^*)\Var_w\big(\text{log-odds}_i\big).
\]
The arbitrage metric is therefore, to second order, a variance of the forecasters' log-odds. Exactly, it is the natural generalization of variance to this geometry.

original: A latent structure is a DAG $\mathcal G$ over hidden nodes $H$ and observed nodes $Y$, and a latent model $\theta$ specifies one conditional table $p_\theta(v\mid\pa_v)$ per node. Two common examples are a single latent $Z$ with the indicators as its children (latent class analysis, or item response theory when $Z$ is continuous), and hierarchical models $Z\to Z_j\to Y_i$. The model predicts $m_\theta(y)=\sum_hp_\theta(h,y)$, and under any proper scoring rule its expected score depends on $\theta$ only through $m_\theta$. So a latent means exactly what it does to predictions of observables; no scoring rule can reward anything else. Two latent models with the same $m_\theta$ are indistinguishable to every score, but there are two quite different ways for this to happen.

To see them, describe a latent model by its \emph{mixing measure}. For each latent state $z$, write down its \emph{profile}, the list of what each indicator would do in that state:
\[
\rho(z)=\big(P(Y_1\mid Z=z),\dots,P(Y_n\mid Z=z)\big).
\]
With binary indicators a profile is a point in the cube $[0,1]^n$. The mixing measure $\nu$ puts mass $P(Z=z)$ on the point $\rho(z)$, and the model's prediction is the $\nu$-weighted average of the corresponding independent distributions, $P(Y)=\int\rho_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_n\,d\nu(\rho)$. A two-state latent class model is two weighted points in the cube; a one-factor IRT model is a curve in the cube, traced out as the factor varies, with a Gaussian spreading mass along it. The \emph{name} of a latent state never appears in $\nu$, only its profile does.

original: \paragraph{Genuine underdetermination: a different $\nu$ with the same average.} Two different clouds can average to the same $P(Y)$. These are different claims about the world, not relabellings. Consider a single binary indicator with $P(Y_1=1)=0.5$. In world (a) the indicator's probability is $0.5$ in every state: the outcome is a genuine coin flip. In world (b) it is $0.9$ half of the time and $0.1$ otherwise: the world is in a decisive state, and we simply do not know which. Both predict the same $P(Y_1)$, but the question ``how often is the world in a state in which $Y_1$ is likely?'' has answer $0$ in (a) and $\tfrac12$ in (b). A continuous example: with two Gaussian indicators of correlation $0.5$ and one factor, the loadings $(0.6,0.833)$, $(0.707,0.707)$ and $(0.9,0.556)$ all reproduce $P(Y)$ exactly and score identically, yet the latent carries $0.97$, $0.79$ and $1.26$ bits of information about $Y$ respectively.

The \emph{unexplained dependence} is the distance to the best model with structure $\mathcal G$,
\[
D_{\mathcal G}=\KL\Big(p(h,y)\,\Big\|\,\textstyle\prod_vp(v\mid\pa_v)\Big)\ \ge0,
\]

It is the scoring rule's half of the story: it is the log-score regret, on complete data, of the best model with structure $\mathcal G$.

\begin{theorem}[the tempered log score elicits the latent bottleneck]\label{arb:thm:stau}
For a single latent,
\[
\min_q\ \mathcal L_\tau(q)=-\max_\theta\ \mathbb E_{y\sim p}\,S_\tau(\theta;y)-\tau\sum_iH(Y_i),
\]
where the minimum is over encoders $q(z\mid y)$. The maximizing $\theta$ is the bottleneck-optimal latent model, and its \emph{tempered posterior} $q(z\mid y)\propto p_\theta(z)\prod_ip_\theta(y_i\mid z)^\tau$ is the optimal encoder. The same holds for a general DAG, with the objective $I(H;Y)+(D_H+\tau D_Y)/(1-\tau)$, where $D_{\mathcal G}=D_H+D_Y$ splits the unexplained dependence into the part among hidden nodes and the rest.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof (single latent)]
All entropies are under the coupling $p(y)\,q(z\mid y)$.
\emph{Step 1.} Using $I(Z;Y)=H(Z)-H(Z\mid Y)$ and $I(Z;Y_i)=H(Y_i)-H(Y_i\mid Z)$,
\[
\mathcal L_\tau(q)+\tau\textstyle\sum_iH(Y_i)=H(Z)+\tau\sum_iH(Y_i\mid Z)-H(Z\mid Y).
\]
\emph{Step 2.} Each entropy is the best achievable expected log loss: $H(Z)=\min_r\mathbb E[-\log r(Z)]$ and $H(Y_i\mid Z)=\min_{c_i}\mathbb E[-\log c_i(Y_i\mid Z)]$, by Gibbs' inequality. A prior $r$ together with indicator conditionals $c_i$ is exactly a latent model $\theta$, so
\[
\mathcal L_\tau(q)+\tau\textstyle\sum_iH(Y_i)=\min_\theta\ \mathbb E\Big[\log q(z\mid y)-\log r(z)-\tau\sum_i\log c_i(y_i\mid z)\Big].
\]
\emph{Step 3.} Now minimize over $q$ as well and exchange the two minimizations. For fixed $\theta$ the bracket separates over $y$ into $\sum_zq(z\mid y)\big[\log q(z\mid y)-\log a_\theta(z,y)\big]$ with $a_\theta(z,y)=r(z)\prod_ic_i(y_i\mid z)^\tau$. This is minimized by $q\propto a_\theta$, with value $-\log\sum_za_\theta(z,y)=-S_\tau(\theta;y)$.
\end{proof}

For one latent with three or more conditionally independent indicators, the decomposition with the fewest latent states is generically unique up to relabelling \citep{kruskalThreewayArraysRank1977,allmanIdentifiabilityParametersLatent2009}, and the same holds for latent trees in which every hidden node has at least three neighbours. In these cases $\tau=1$ already elicits the true latent, and EM recovers it. Even here, however, parsimony is a convention: uniqueness holds among models with the fewest \emph{states}, and the latent with the fewest \emph{bits} can differ. In exact computations, the least-information latent was cheaper than the true one in all ten random two-indicator models and in all four three-binary-indicator models tried, and equal to it with three ternary indicators or once a fourth indicator was added. More indicators shrink the set of exact fits until the convention stops mattering; we conjecture, on the basis of these computations, that this happens in general once the indicators are rich enough.

Three of the design options it discusses are more problematic.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{A free-form latent distribution} (letting traders ``drag around'' the latent distribution). Payouts depend on the latent only through the joint distribution of the indicators. For a Gaussian latent $P(Z>1)=0.156$, but every latent distribution giving the same indicator joint earns identical payouts, and among these $P(Z>1)$ ranges over $[0.040,0.317]$ with three indicators, $[0.078,0.253]$ with six and $[0.087,0.237]$ with ten. Traders can move such beliefs at no expected cost or reward. The remedy is to keep the latent distribution parametric, or to settle with $S_\tau$ and accept the compression.
\item \emph{Several latent factors.} This is not in fact a defect. Rotating the loadings together with the factors changes nothing observable: it is gauge, not missing information. Which axis represents ``who is winning'' is a choice of coordinates, not a fact, so a market cannot price it and should not try. Such quantities should be defined relationally, for example as ``the latent direction along which the probability of indicator 3 rises fastest'', and these are priced whenever the model is identified up to rotation.
\item \emph{User-proposed latent classes.} The log score never penalizes an extra class, since a model with $k+1$ classes contains every model with $k$. A redundant class ties with the true model (the $S_1$ column of \cref{arb:tab:incentives}), and the latent drifts towards being ``the indicators themselves''. Settling with $S_\tau$ for $\tau$ slightly below one makes every proposed class pay for its bits, which answers the proposal's open question of who should choose the number of classes: a class stays exactly when it raises $S_\tau$.
\end{enumerate}

original: \paragraph{Bayesian-network markets.} The combinatorial markets of \citet{sunProbabilityAssetUpdating2012} and \citet{laskeyGraphicalModelMarket2018} allow traders to edit both the parameters and the structure of a Bayesian network, including adding variables. A latent node can certainly be represented. But each trade is paid as an edit to the joint distribution of the variables it touches, settled when those variables resolve. If a trader raises $P(Z)$ while leaving $P(Y\mid Z)$ unchanged, its gain in each state is $b\log\frac{q(Z)}{p(Z)}$, which depends on $Z$ itself; when the observables resolve, the market updates its beliefs about $Z$, but nothing settles that contract. A trader can still profit before settlement by selling once the evidence has moved the price, but no rule pays it for its contribution to the observable predictions if $Z$ never resolves. The latent-variable market avoids this by scoring the change in the \emph{observable} marginal, with $Z$ integrated out, and the deep market of \cref{arb:sec:latent-goods} does the same thing in economic language: the latent node is an intermediate good, and its price is derived from the consumers downstream.

We return to the measure of inconsistency in \Cref{ch:arbitrage} to show that it corresponds to what a market of arbitragists would compute.

original: For alignment the gap matters a great deal. Interpretability asks what a model believes internally, and eliciting latent knowledge asks how to get a model to report those beliefs honestly rather than what it predicts a human would say \citep{christianoElicitingLatentKnowledge2021}. Human values are themselves functions of latent variables: we care whether people are flourishing, not whether some measurable proxy for it goes up. raw: Latent variables are interesting for elicitation for at least two reasons. original: From the economic point of view of \cref{part:agency}, one would expect latent beliefs to be produced like anything else in an economy. A belief about a latent variable is useful because it improves predictions and decisions downstream, so its value, and with it how much subsidy a market for that latent deserves, should be set by price recursion. Yet there is no obvious market mechanism that elicits latent beliefs, still less one that creates markets for new latent variables as they become useful. Humans and AI systems nonetheless form latent beliefs all the time.
raw: What would markets look like if latent variables were just another kind of commodity? In this framework, a belief about a latent variable is useful insofar as it helps with downstream forecasting or decision-making, so it makes sense to think that the correct amount of subsidy for markets about latents will be given by price recursion. But what market mechanism elicits beliefs about latents? What market mechanism creates markets about latents as needed?
humanized: From the economic point of view of \cref{part:agency}, one would expect latent beliefs to be produced like anything else in an economy. Recursively setting prices this way would give us a principled way of figuring out which latent beliefs we should care about eliciting. Unfortunately, we don't currently have a good way to do this. People and AIs have latent beliefs all the time, but we don't have a good mechanism for eliciting them, let alone one that spins up markets for new latent variables when appropriate.

original: Two existing proposals come close. Combinatorial prediction markets built on Bayesian networks \citep{sunProbabilityAssetUpdating2012,laskeyGraphicalModelMarket2018} let traders edit both the parameters and the structure of a network, so a latent node can be represented; but a trade in such a market is settled when the variables it concerns resolve, and a latent variable never does, so nothing pays a trader for what its latent belief contributes to the predictions of observables. Latent-variable prediction markets \citep{tailcalledLatentVariablesPrediction2023} fix this by paying traders according to the change in the predicted probability of the observable indicators, with the latent integrated out. This has sound incentives, but it leaves the latent beliefs themselves partly unpriced. Some of the freedom is harmless (relabelling a latent, or rotating several latent factors into one another, changes nothing anyone could check), but some is not: when the latent distribution or the number of latent classes is left to the traders, quite different latent models earn exactly the same payouts.
raw: Bayesian network prediction markets [[	extbackslash citep{sunProbabilityAssetUpdating2012,laskeyGraphicalModelMarket2018}] allow traders to update parameters and the structure of a Bayesian network, which can in principle include latent nodes; but a trade in a combinatorial prediction market pays out based on the eventual resolutions of the random variables it includes, and latent variables never resolve, so this doesn’t give traders an incentive to correctly price in their knowledge of how latents influence the distribution over observables. Latent-variable prediction markets [[	extbackslash citep{tailcalledLatentVariablesPrediction2023}]] get around this problem by paying out traders based on the effect of their updates on the probability predicted for indicator events, marginalizing out latent variables; this gives traders the right incentives but doesn’t fully price in all aspects of beliefs about latents. Some degrees of freedom don’t matter, for instance, how traders name their latent variables, or rotate their coordinate system in a space of latent factors, but other degrees of freedom do: if we allow traders to make updates to the distribution over latent variables (including the number of latent classes), very different beliefs about latents give rise to the same payouts.
humanized: There are two existing mechanisms that come close, though. Bayesian networks can model latent (unobserved) variables. In a prediction market based on a Bayesian network \citep{sunProbabilityAssetUpdating2012,laskeyGraphicalModelMarket2018}, traders are able to modify the parameters and even the structure of the network (and hence introduce latent variables). However, in such markets, traders make predictions about observables only, since markets are resolved when the relevant variables are observed. Thus, the part of a trader's belief about the network that concerns latent variables, even to the extent that it affects his predictions about observables, does not earn him anything in such markets. Another class of prediction markets \citep{tailcalledLatentVariablesPrediction2023} deals with this issue by having traders place their bets on indicators (which are functions of the latent variable and possibly other variables). Traders are rewarded based on how well they predict the indicators (integrating out the latent variable). This has nice incentive properties, but only partially prices latent beliefs. Some degrees of freedom don't matter (e.g. traders could consistently relabel the latent classes or rotate some latent variables into each other in ways no one could detect), but some do: e.g. traders could pick a very different distribution over latents, or even the number of latent classes, and no one would notice since both versions would result in the same payments.
final: There are two existing mechanisms that come close. Bayesian networks can model latent (unobserved) variables. In a combinatorial prediction market based on a Bayesian network \citep{sunProbabilityAssetUpdating2012,laskeyGraphicalModelMarket2018}, traders are able to modify the parameters and even the structure of the network, so a latent node can be represented. However, a trade in such a market is settled when the variables it concerns resolve, and a latent variable never does. Thus the part of a trader's belief that concerns latent variables earns it nothing, even to the extent that it contributes to its predictions of observables. Latent-variable prediction markets \citep{tailcalledLatentVariablesPrediction2023} deal with this issue by rewarding traders according to the change in the predicted probability of the observable indicators, with the latent variable integrated out. This has sound incentive properties, but only partially prices latent beliefs. Some degrees of freedom do not matter (relabelling a latent, or rotating several latent factors into one another, changes nothing anyone could detect), but some do: when the distribution over latents or the number of latent classes is left to the traders, quite different latent models result in exactly the same payments.

original: In \cref{ch:arbitrage} we show that the arbitrage metric of \cref{ch:consistency} is exactly the welfare gained by trade in a market of quasi-linear consumers, that the arbitraged forecasts are the market's equilibrium prices, and that the arbitraged combination of utilities is utilitarian welfare, the objective assumed in \cref{ch:agency}. In markets over dependent questions, the prices of worlds are the arbitrageur's profits, and latent variables are \emph{intermediate goods} priced by price recursion; a market whose routers follow proportional response learns them by EM. We then argue that a latent belief means exactly what it does to predictions of observables, separate the harmless (gauge) part of what scoring leaves free from the genuine part, and introduce the \emph{latent bottleneck}, which asks latents to explain the observables with as few bits as possible. Its optimum can be elicited from a single outcome with a new scoring rule, the \emph{tempered log score}. Finally we use these results to assess latent-variable and Bayesian-network prediction markets.
raw: In [[	extbackslash cref{ch:arbitrage}]][[	extbackslash cref{ch:consistency}]] we define a notion of consistency between probabilistic forecasts, and prove that the metric induced by arbitrage is exactly the welfare improvement from allowing trades between agents with quasi-linear utilities. The forecasts that cannot be improved via arbitrage are exactly the prices in a market equilibrium. The forecast resulting from arbitraging away disagreements between agents’ utilities is exactly the utilitarian social welfare function (which we use in [[	extbackslash cref{ch:agency}]]). We propose one such scoring rule, the [[	extbackslash emph{tempered log score}]], which incentivizes traders to compress the observable events into as few bits as possible (passing through an information [[	extbackslash emph{latent bottleneck}]]); the optimum of this scoring rule can be elicited even from a single realized outcome. We then apply this framework to analyze Bayesian-network and latent-variable prediction markets. In combinatorial prediction markets over logically-related questions, the price of each possible world is given by the profit of arbitraging it away; latent variables are [[	extbackslash emph{intermediate goods}]], and their prices are given by price recursion. In particular, if traders route flow using proportional response, the market learns prices for latent variables using EM.
humanized: In \cref{ch:arbitrage} we show that in a market of quasi-linear consumers, the arbitrage metric of \cref{ch:consistency} is exactly the welfare gained by trade, the arbitraged forecasts are the market's equilibrium prices, and the arbitraged combination of utilities is utilitarian welfare, the objective assumed in \cref{ch:agency}. In such markets, arbitrageurs' profits are equal to the prices of worlds. The latent variables \emph{intermediate goods} can be priced with a price recursion. In particular, EM can be implemented by a market whose routers use proportional response. We argue that all a latent belief means is what it does to predictions of observables, disentangle the (harmless, gauge) freedom that scoring leaves from what is real, and motivate \emph{latent bottleneck}, which requires the latents to explain the observables using as few bits as possible. Its optimum can be elicited from a single outcome with a new scoring rule, the \emph{tempered log score}. Finally, we'll use these results to analyze latent-variable and Bayesian-network prediction markets.
final: In \cref{ch:arbitrage} we show that in a market of quasi-linear consumers, the arbitrage metric of \cref{ch:consistency} is exactly the welfare gained by trade, the arbitraged forecasts are the market's equilibrium prices, and the arbitraged combination of utilities is utilitarian welfare, the objective assumed in \cref{ch:agency}. In markets over dependent questions, the prices of worlds are equal to the arbitrageur's profits, and latent variables are \emph{intermediate goods}, priced by price recursion; a market whose routers use proportional response learns them by EM. We argue that all a latent belief means is what it does to predictions of observables, separate the harmless (gauge) part of the freedom that scoring leaves from the genuine part, and introduce the \emph{latent bottleneck}, which requires the latents to explain the observables using as few bits as possible. Its optimum can be elicited from a single outcome with a new scoring rule, the \emph{tempered log score}. Finally, we use these results to analyze latent-variable and Bayesian-network prediction markets.

original: Proper scoring rules reward a probabilistic forecast according to the outcome that occurs, in such a way that reporting one's true belief maximizes expected reward \citep{goodRationalDecisions1952,savageElicitationPersonalProbabilities1971,gneitingStrictlyProperScoring2007}. Market scoring rules turn a scoring rule into an automated market maker: each trader is paid the difference between the score of the price it leaves and the score of the price it found, so the market maker's total loss is bounded by the score of the initial price \citep{hansonLogarithmicMarketScoring2002,hansonCombinatorialInformationMarket2003}. Market makers of this kind are equivalent to cost-function market makers, whose prices are the gradient of a convex cost function and whose scoring rule is its convex conjugate \citep{chenUtilityFrameworkBoundedloss2007,abernethyEfficientMarketMaking2013}. With traders of constant absolute risk aversion, the equilibrium price aggregates beliefs as a risk-tolerance-weighted geometric average, a result that goes back to the theory of syndicates \citep{wilsonTheorySyndicates1968,abernethyInformationAggregationExponential2014}. All of these mechanisms require that the event eventually resolves. \citet{conitzerPredictionMarketsMechanism2012} studies how to reward agents for the information they bring to a market, but again only where the market is eventually settled against ground truth.

Market scoring rules are equivalent to a certain class of cost-function market makers, where prices are the gradient of a convex cost function and the scoring rule is the convex conjugate of the cost function [[\citep{chenUtilityFrameworkBoundedloss2007,abernethyEfficientMarketMaking2013}]]. Market scoring rules bound the total losses of the market maker in terms of the score at the starting price. When traders have CARA (constant absolute risk aversion) utility functions, the equilibrium price aggregates trader beliefs via a risk-tolerance-weighted geometric average; this dates back to the theory of syndicates [[\citep{wilsonTheorySyndicates1968,abernethyInformationAggregationExponential2014}]]. [[\citep{conitzerPredictionMarketsMechanism2012}]] studies mechanisms for paying agents according to the value of the information they provide in such markets. original: Combinatorial prediction markets let traders bet on Boolean combinations of events and on conditional events, so that the market maintains a joint distribution over many related questions \citep{hansonCombinatorialInformationMarket2003}. Pricing such a market exactly is computationally hard in general, which has led to market makers that represent the joint distribution as a Bayesian network and restrict trades to those that preserve its structure \citep{pennock2012PriceUpdatingCombinatorialPredictionMarketsBayesianNetworks,sunProbabilityAssetUpdating2012}. The most developed of these, deployed in the DAGGRE and SciCast forecasting markets, also lets traders add variables and dependencies, and so crowdsources the structure of the network as well as its parameters \citep{laskeyGraphicalModelMarket2018}. The dynamics of traders in such markets can be analysed as randomized coordinate descent \citep{frongilloConvergenceAnalysisPrediction2015}. Latent-variable prediction markets \citep{tailcalledLatentVariablesPrediction2023} instead let traders move the parameters of an item-response or latent-class model over a set of indicator questions, paying them by the change in the log-likelihood of the indicators once these resolve.

In this part we'll also study prediction markets over combinations of questions (rather than over single questions). In combinatorial prediction markets \citep{hansonCombinatorialInformationMarket2003}, traders can trade on conditional events or Boolean combinations of events, so the market maker maintains a joint distribution over events. Since pricing is computationally challenging, some combinatorial prediction market market makers maintain a distribution factorized according to a Bayesian network, and allow only those trades which maintain that factorization \citep{pennock2012PriceUpdatingCombinatorialPredictionMarketsBayesianNetworks,sunProbabilityAssetUpdating2012}. One such market maker, which has been used in the DAGGRE and SciCast forecasting markets, also allows traders to make trades which introduce new variables and dependencies; in this way, traders not only provide parameter estimates, they also crowdsource the graphical structure of the Bayesian network \citep{laskeyGraphicalModelMarket2018}. Trading dynamics in combinatorial prediction markets can be analyzed as forms of coordinate descent \citep{frongilloConvergenceAnalysisPrediction2015}.

original: \Cref{ch:intro} argued that economies are agents built out of much simpler agents, and that this suggests an economic theory of agency. The most direct way to test that suggestion is to build an agent that literally is a market: a reinforcement learner whose actions are decided by an internal economy of sub-agents, each paid out of the rewards its decisions eventually bring in. Such agents are not new. Holland's classifier systems and Baum's Hayek machine already worked this way, and the idea of evaluating a market as an intelligence goes back further still. But all of them auction the entire world to a single winner at each step, which is precisely what real markets do not do. A real economy has many goods, owned and traded separately, and much of its power comes from that division.

The most literal way of following up on that idea is to build agents that are economies: reinforcement learners who delegate decisions to internal sub-agents, rewarded according to the payoffs their choices have on the parent agent's environment. This idea is not new: it shows up in Holland's classifier systems and Baum's Hayek machine, and has a long history of being used to evaluate markets as theories of intelligence. These algorithms all auction off the entire world to a single agent at each decision step, however. That's not very economical! Economies have many different goods which are owned and traded independently of each other, and some of their power may come from that separation.

original: This chapter takes that difference seriously. It sets out a common framework for market-based agents on top of a partially observed Markov decision process, recovers the existing algorithms as \emph{deep} markets, in which a single good (the state) passes from owner to owner, and introduces \emph{wide} markets, in which the state is itself split into separately traded goods. It then looks at what such agents might be good for: searching over plans, growing or shrinking with the problem, and giving every component complete feedback. Along the way a link to neural networks appears: prices in an equilibrium market can be computed by something that looks like backpropagation. That link is suggestive rather than natural, and making it precise is the job of the next chapter. Since the chapter began as a position paper, its arguments are often informal, and it should be read as a map of the territory that the rest of \cref{part:agency} explores more carefully.
humanized: In this chapter, we'll describe market-based agents in terms of a partially observed Markov decision process. In that setting, we can reinterpret existing algorithms as \emph{deep} markets, in which there's just one good, the state, and ownership of that good changes hands every timestep. original: Experiments, however, need a measure of success, and the measure used so far, the accuracy of the judge's final answer, is not the one that matters for alignment. An economist asks of a mechanism whether it gives participants the right incentives; for oversight, that means whether the protocol rewards an agent more for arguing the truth than for arguing a falsehood. A protocol can make the judge accurate without doing this, for instance if the judge simply trusts an agent who happens to be honest. This chapter builds the benchmark around incentives instead. It introduces the Agent Score Difference, which measures how much a protocol favours truth over falsehood, formalizes a general class of protocol experiments in a Python library, and uses both to compare Debate, Consultancy and a simple model of RLHF. Like every empirical study of oversight so far, the benchmark relies on questions whose answers are known, a limitation that points to the questions taken up in \cref{part:subjective}.

But for alignment what we ultimately care about is whether the system is providing good incentives: will the more intelligent agent get a higher reward from arguing falsehoods or arguing the truth? This is an economist's question! An unintelligent judge could get highly accurate answers by delegating all questions to a single honest butchler agent, but that would not be giving good incentives.
